criteria.descriptor: Correctly explains that ~96% accuracy is the majority-class baseline at 4% prevalence, correctly diagnoses image-level splitting as patient-level leakage, and names appropriate metrics (sensitivity/specificity/precision/PR-AUC) with accurate reasoning for why PR-AUC is preferable to ROC-AUC under imbalance. No false claims (e.g., that resampling the test set is acceptable, or that ROC-AUC 0.94 alone proves readiness).

Addresses all three problem areas -- metric choice, the split/leakage flaw, and operating-point selection -- plus at least one of uncertainty quantification, realistic test prevalence, external validation, or calibration.

Justifies each fix mechanistically (quantifies the trivial-classifier baseline, explains why grouped splitting removes leakage, ties the threshold choice to a clinical sensitivity target) rather than merely listing remedies.
Presents a clear critique-then-protocol structure using precise evaluation vocabulary, pairing each identified flaw with a concrete, actionable fix.

expected_answer_points: Accuracy is uninformative at ~4% prevalence: a trivial always-negative classifier already scores ~96%, so the reported accuracy is just the majority-class baseline.
Report class-appropriate metrics instead -- sensitivity/recall, specificity, precision, F1, and especially PR-AUC (average precision) focused on the minority positive class.
ROC-AUC can be optimistic/misleading under severe imbalance because it is dominated by the large negative class; PR-AUC is the more informative threshold-free summary here.

Image-level splitting with ~5 images per patient causes patient-level data leakage (the same patient in train and test), inflating test scores; the fix is a patient/group-level split (GroupKFold or grouped hold-out).

Threshold-free AUC alone is insufficient: choose a clinically meaningful operating point/threshold (e.g., a target sensitivity) and report the confusion matrix, sensitivity, specificity, and precision at it.
Report uncertainty (e.g., bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, resampling over patients) given the small number of positives.

Keep realistic prevalence in the test set (do not resample/rebalance it) and validate against distribution shift via an external/held-out population, optionally checking calibration (reliability diagram/ECE), before declaring deployment readiness.
common_pitfalls: Only swaps accuracy for F1 (or PR-AUC) while ignoring the patient-level leakage in the split, which is the larger error.
Takes the 0.94 ROC-AUC at face value as proof the model works, missing that ROC-AUC is inflated/uninformative when positives are only ~4%.
Proposes k-fold cross-validation but still splits at the image level, so the patient leakage persists.
Suggests oversampling/SMOTE or class-rebalancing the test set to 'fix' the imbalance, which corrupts the evaluation by distorting the real prevalence.
Reports only threshold-free metrics and never selects an operating point or reports a confusion matrix / sensitivity at a usable threshold.
Omits uncertainty (confidence intervals) and external validation, treating a single internal test number as deployment-ready.
reference_answer:
The evaluation has three serious flaws.

1) Metric mismatch under class imbalance. With ~4% positives, a model that predicts 'no DR' for every image already scores ~96% accuracy, so the reported accuracy is the majority-class baseline and tells us nothing. The relevant quantities are sensitivity (recall) and specificity, precision, and F1 for the positive class, summarized threshold-free by PR-AUC (average precision). A 0.94 ROC-AUC looks strong, but under heavy imbalance ROC-AUC is dominated by the large negative class and can stay high even when precision on the minority class is poor; PR-AUC is the more honest summary here.

2) Data leakage from the split. With ~5 images per patient, an image-level split puts images from the same patient in both train and test. The network can exploit patient-specific features, so the test score is optimistically biased. Split at the patient (group) level -- GroupKFold or a grouped hold-out keyed on patient id -- so no patient straddles the boundary.

3) No operating point and no uncertainty. Threshold-free AUCs don't describe how the deployed system behaves. Pick a threshold on the validation set at a clinically required sensitivity (e.g., 90%), then report the test confusion matrix with sensitivity, specificity, and precision at that point. Report 95% confidence intervals (bootstrap resampling over patients, not images) because the number of positive patients is small.

Protocol: patient-level grouped split (or grouped CV); keep prevalence realistic in the test set -- never resample or rebalance the test set; report PR-AUC plus sensitivity/specificity/precision at a pre-committed operating point with bootstrap CIs; check calibration (reliability diagram / ECE) if the probabilities are used clinically; and validate on an external site/camera population to probe distribution shift before claiming deployment readiness.
